paras: The lynching of Reimheimer was the hanging of a German man, his name printed as Reimheimer and in several other spellings, by a band of about twenty to twenty-five unknown men who took him from the jail at Rockport, Atchison County, Missouri, early on June 11, 1881.
He had been accused of shooting and robbing a man named Albert Angel near Irish Grove six days earlier, and he was awaiting trial when he was seized.
A St. Joseph dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, often in news summaries beside the lynching of a Black man, John Taylor, in North Carolina the same weekend.
According to the St. Joseph dispatch, Albert Angel was shot and robbed of $250 near Irish Grove, Atchison County, on June 5, and the man accused of the crime then rode off on one of Angel's horses.
The St. Joe News, as reprinted in Sedalia, added that the accused man was caught at Clarinda, Iowa, and brought back to Rockport for trial.
The papers called him only "a German" and gave no first name.
About one o'clock in the morning, some twenty unknown men forced their way into the Rockport jail, took the prisoner out and hanged him to a tree.
The Sedalia account put the band at about twenty-five men and said they carried him a mile and a half from town before hanging him.
The same account said that Sheriff Gray, who was returning from Jefferson City with a requisition from the governor, hurried to Rockport to prevent violence but arrived too late.
Angel was reported to be recovering from his wound.
No report of an inquest, an arrest or a prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The Chicago Daily Tribune printed the St. Joseph dispatch on June 12 under the single word "LYNCHED", and the fuller version, credited to the St. Louis Republican's St. Joseph correspondent, ran on June 13 in the Wheeling Register as "A Missouri Lynching" and in the Alexandria Gazette.
The Portland Daily Press headed a shorter version "Short Work with a Horse Thief", which reduced the charge to stealing a horse and robbing its owner and named no town.

The Savannah Morning News grouped it with the North Carolina case under "JUDGE LYNCH. A Negro Strung Up in North Carolina and a German Hanged in Missouri", and a general-news summary run by the Daily Gazette, the Lancaster Intelligencer, the Daily Republican and the Westminster Democratic Advocate set the two lynchings side by side in consecutive sentences.

German-language papers in Ohio printed translations, one under the heading "Ein Deutscher 'gelyncht'", and in Missouri the Kirksville Weekly Graphic gave the story one sentence calling the lynchers "vigilants".
None of the reports condemned the lynching; most stated the accusation against the prisoner as fact and ended with Angel's prospects for recovery.
Later rural news digests in Mississippi and Tennessee and the Ebensburg Cambria Freeman in Pennsylvania carried the story into the following week.

The reports differ on when the hanging took place: the dispatches dated June 11 said "this morning" at about one o'clock, the Weekly Graphic said "Friday night", the Mississippi and Tennessee digests said "the 10th", and the Sedalia paper said Saturday night between twelve and one.
Because the wire reports were filed on June 11 and describe the event as that morning, the night of June 10-11 is the best-supported date.

The Portland Daily Press and the Savannah Morning News named no town for the jail, so their St. Joseph dateline was read by some as the place of the lynching; every report that names the jail places it at Rockport.

bases: About twenty to twenty-five unknown men took an accused man from the Rockport jail and hanged him (A1, A6, A16).

A band of some twenty (A1, A6) or twenty-five (A16) unknown men forcibly took a prisoner awaiting trial for shooting and robbery from jail and hanged him, punishing an alleged crime outside the law; the victim is described only as 'a German', not as Black.

The St. Louis Republican's St. Joseph special (A1, A6), the St. Joe News account reprinted at Sedalia (A16) and the Weekly Graphic's state brief (A11) agree that Reimheimer was taken from the Rockport jail and hanged.

accounts.gist: 'Vigilants' at Rockport took him from the jail on Friday night and hanged him.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the St. Joseph dispatch or a one-sentence summary without comment, stating the accusation as fact.
The Portland Daily Press's 'Short Work with a Horse Thief' and the Savannah Morning News's 'JUDGE LYNCH' headline treated the hanging as summary justice, without condemnation.
Missouri papers gave brief state-news items, the Weekly Graphic calling the lynchers 'vigilants' and the Sedalia Bazoo noting the sheriff's late arrival 'unfortunately'.
